one_line_idea: The gradient noise scale of dense training drifts by an order of magnitude within a single run (unlike classification's comparative stability), so any fixed batch size is wrong for most of the run and a noise-tracking batch-size ramp captures measurable gains.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Dense tasks concentrate late-phase learning in small pixel populations (boundaries, rare classes), collapsing the effective sample count per batch as interiors saturate; the gradient noise scale therefore rises steeply within-run, meaning early training is over-batched (wasted parallelism) and late training under-batched (noise-limited), and a batch ramp tracking measured noise achieves better accuracy-per-FLOP than any fixed batch.

one_line_idea: Photometric augmentation strength and learning rate are partially interchangeable noise sources in dense training, with iso-accuracy contours revealing a measurable exchange rate, so recipes tuned at one LR silently mis-tune augmentation at another.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Label-preserving photometric augmentation perturbs gradients much like extra minibatch noise; since SGD's implicit regularization depends on total noise level, augmentation strength and LR trade off along iso-accuracy contours in the (LR, aug-strength) plane with a quantifiable negative-slope exchange band, until augmentation begins destroying task-relevant information and the contours collapse.

one_line_idea: Channel dropout and spatially structured dropout in dense decoders trade places as decoder width changes, because their effective noise targets (feature redundancy vs spatial redundancy) scale oppositely with width, predicting a width-conditioned reversal that folklore misses.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Channel dropout regularizes against inter-channel co-adaptation, which grows with decoder width, while spatial dropout regularizes against local spatial co-adaptation, which is width-independent; therefore narrow decoders benefit more from spatial variants (channel dropout destroys scarce capacity) and wide decoders from channel variants, producing a systematic ranking reversal at a measurable width threshold.

one_line_idea: Stochastic depth in ViT dense fine-tuning is an implicit layer-wise LR decay in disguise (deeper blocks receive fewer effective updates), so its tuned drop-rate profile should be reproducible by an explicit LLRD profile matched to expected update rates, unifying two rituals.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Skipping a block removes its update that step, so a linearly increasing drop-rate profile multiplies each block's expected update count by its keep probability, exactly what LLRD does deterministically; if the regularization-relevant variable is per-block effective update budget, then LLRD matched to the keep-probability profile reproduces stochastic depth's accuracy, and their combination is redundant (no additive gain).

one_line_idea: Label smoothing in segmentation trades boundary representation quality for interior stability: it collapses the logit structure that encodes soft class transitions at boundaries, predicting opposite effects on interior and boundary metrics that aggregate mIoU conceals.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] At true class transitions, unsmoothed training lets logits encode graded mixtures (an honest representation of boundary pixels); smoothing forces all pixels toward the same target geometry, erasing the graded structure and pushing boundary decisions toward hard, spatially unstable transitions, so boundary-band accuracy and transition-zone logit entropy structure degrade while interior accuracy mildly improves from the regularization.

one_line_idea: The ramp-up period folklore for auxiliary regularizer weights exists to protect training until the supervised gradient stabilizes, so an adaptive ramp triggered by measured gradient-norm stabilization should match hand-tuned ramps across setups with zero tuning.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] The ramp's function is to keep auxiliary pressure weak while the supervised gradient field is still large and rapidly rotating (early chaos), and to reach full strength once supervised dynamics stabilize; the correct ramp clock is therefore the measured stabilization of supervised gradient statistics (norm and direction change rate), not step count, so an adaptive ramp keyed to that signal transfers across datasets, budgets, and LR schedules without re-tuning.

one_line_idea: Wide random-resize ranges pay their cost only early: scale-range annealing (wide early, narrow late) should match full wide-range training on scale robustness while recovering the late-phase accuracy that wide ranges tax, resolving the scale-augmentation dilemma as a scheduling problem.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Scale diversity teaches scale-robust features, a structural property acquired early and retained; late in training, wide scale jitter mostly injects gradient variance that impedes fine consolidation without adding robustness, so annealing the range concentrates diversity where it builds structure and calm where consolidation needs it, dominating any fixed range on the joint (robustness, accuracy) frontier.

one_line_idea: Weight decay and strong augmentation regularize an overlapping subspace in dense training (both suppress feature-norm growth on nuisance directions), predicting substitutability with a measurable exchange rate and explaining why heavily augmented recipes tolerate near-zero decay.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Both mechanisms limit the model's ability to amplify sample-specific nuisance directions (decay by shrinking all weights, augmentation by making nuisance features unreliable across views); on the shared subspace they are substitutes, so iso-accuracy contours in the (decay, augmentation-strength) plane will show a broad substitution band, with decay mattering most exactly when augmentation is weak, and the two failing to substitute only on augmentation-blind directions (e.g., features invariant to the augmentation family used).

one_line_idea: Geometric augmentations (flips, rotations) and photometric augmentations act on dense training through different optimization channels, geometric ones reshaping the per-pixel loss landscape correlation structure and photometric ones adding gradient noise, predicting non-interchangeable, task-dependent roles that strength-matching experiments will separate.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Photometric transforms leave the spatial supervision structure intact (same pixels, same geometry), acting as label-preserving gradient noise; geometric transforms re-map the correspondence between network equivariance structure and supervision, decorrelating per-pixel gradients across views and specifically training spatial-equivariance pathways; consequently, matched-strength substitutions will fail asymmetrically: geometric-for-photometric substitution preserves noise benefits but photometric-for-geometric cannot restore equivariance training, showing up as task-dependent irreplaceability (geometry-heavy tasks like depth suffer more from losing geometric augmentation).

one_line_idea: Loss spikes in dense training are triggered by reproducible image-crop-augmentation conjunctions, not random batch bad luck: the same content configurations spike across seeds, making spike-trigger mining a dataset diagnostic rather than a stability mystery.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Spikes arise when specific content meets specific transformation states (extreme crops of unusual structures, augmentation pushing inputs outside learned statistics); these conjunctions are properties of the data-augmentation distribution, not of the stochastic trajectory, so spike triggers replicate across seeds and identify a stable pathological subdistribution whose characterization explains what the model cannot yet absorb at each phase.

one_line_idea: Backbone parameters in dense training sit at the edge of stability (top curvature hovering near the 2/LR boundary) like classification networks do, but dense decoder heads systematically do not, revealing a two-regime landscape that schedule design currently ignores.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] The per-pixel averaged loss gives decoder heads much smaller and spatially diffuse curvature contributions, while shared backbones accumulate curvature from all pixels; module-resolved curvature tracking will show backbones at the stability edge (curvature rides the 2/LR line) while decoders sit far below it, implying decoders are effectively under-stepped at the global LR and could absorb larger module-wise steps, a structural inefficiency in every single-LR dense recipe.

one_line_idea: Divergence events in ViT dense fine-tuning are preceded by attention-entropy collapse in a small identifiable set of heads, providing an early-warning signal several hundred steps ahead of the loss explosion and a targeted intervention (per-head temperature) that prevents it.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] In dense fine-tuning, divergence is seeded when particular heads (typically high-resolution, late-block heads processing boundary-dense tokens) sharpen toward near-deterministic attention; the entropy collapse of those heads precedes global loss explosion by a detectable margin, and clamping only the collapsing heads' attention temperature interrupts the cascade at negligible accuracy cost, establishing causality rather than correlation.

one_line_idea: Recovery from training spikes is spatially unequal: interior and frequent-class accuracy heals within hundreds of steps while rare-class and boundary accuracy exhibits hysteresis lasting many epochs, so a run's spike history taxes exactly the metrics that aggregate curves hide.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Spikes disproportionately corrupt low-redundancy knowledge (rare-class prototypes, fine boundary placements) whose gradient signal is too sparse to rebuild quickly, while high-redundancy knowledge (frequent-class interiors) re-converges almost immediately; therefore post-spike deficits persist selectively, spike-heavy runs end measurably worse on rare/boundary metrics at matched final aggregate loss, and a short post-spike replay of rare-class-dense content erases the selective deficit.
